a: The proverbs of Solomon.
p: The second heading opens a collection that runs to 22:16. Its verses add up to the number value of Solomon's name.
b: After nine chapters of long speeches, 10:1 starts again with "The proverbs of Solomon" (compare 1:1) and changes form: from here to 22:16 almost every verse is a two-line saying that stands on its own. The collection has 375 verses, and the Hebrew letters of Solomon's name, Shelomoh, add up to 375 (300 + 30 + 40 + 5). Patrick Skehan argued that an editor counted the sayings on purpose. Most scholars divide the collection in two: in chapters 10–15 the second line usually turns against the first with "but"; in 16:1–22:16 the two lines more often say the same thing twice or build on each other. On Solomon and the headings, see the introduction to the book.

a: A wise son makes a father glad,
p: The collection opens, as the speeches of 1–9 did, with a son and both his parents.
b: The first saying names both parents, as the speeches do (1:8; 6:20). The father is glad; the mother bears the grief. Hebrew poetry often splits one idea across the two lines, so the point is that a son's character touches both parents, not that only mothers suffer. The same opening line returns at 15:20, so the two sayings frame the first half of the collection. The family is the first school in Proverbs, and the sayings that follow keep coming back to a son who listens and a son who will not (13:1; 15:5; 17:21, 25; 19:26; 23:24–25; 29:3).

a: righteousness rescues from death
p: In later Hebrew tsedaqah came to mean giving to the poor, and the rabbis read this line that way.
b: Tsedaqah in Proverbs means right living and fair dealing, the opposite of "treasures won by wickedness". The line says such a life is safer than ill-gotten wealth, which cannot buy off death (11:4 repeats it). By the time of the rabbis the same word had come to mean alms, giving to the poor, and the Talmud reads "tsedaqah rescues from death" as a promise about charity: the story is told of Rabbi Akiva's daughter, spared from a snake on her wedding night because she had fed a poor man (Bavli Shabbat 156b; compare Bava Batra 10a). Tobit, a book Scripture for Catholics and Orthodox, says the same of almsgiving (Tobit 4:10; Tobit 12:9). The modern Jewish word for charity, tsedakah, carries this history.

a: One who brings the crop in during summer
p: The farming year set the rhythm of life, and a son who slept through harvest let the family's food rot in the field.
b: Israel's grain harvest came in spring and early summer, and the summer fruit (chiefly figs, along with grapes) later in the dry season; the olives came last, in autumn. The Gezer Calendar, a schoolboy's tablet of about the 900s BC, lists the farming months: months of olive harvest, sowing, late planting, flax, barley harvest, the harvest "and measuring", vine pruning and "summer fruit" (qayits, the word in this verse). The work could not wait: a crop left in the field spoiled or was eaten. So the sayings about lazy and hard-working people (10:4–5, 26; 12:11, 24, 27; 13:4) are about whether a household eats, not only about character. The ant of 6:6–8 makes the same point.

a: the mouth of the wicked keeps violence covered
p: The Hebrew can mean the wicked hide violence in their talk, or that violence will cover their mouths.
b: The verb "covers" has no marked subject. Either the mouth of the wicked covers (hides) violence behind smooth words, or violence covers the mouth of the wicked, like a shroud or a gag (the KJV's "violence covereth the mouth of the wicked"). The second reading makes a better contrast with blessings resting on the head of the righteous; the first fits 10:11, where the same line is set against a mouth that is a spring of life. The collectors reused whole half-lines like this one (10:8b and 10:10b are another pair), which shows they worked from a store of stock lines.
orig: וּפִי רְשָׁעִים יְכַסֶּה חָמָס (ufi resha'im yekhasseh chamas)

a: The righteous are remembered with blessing,
p: Jews still add "may his memory be a blessing" after the name of someone who has died. The phrase comes from this verse.
b: The Hebrew zekher tsaddiq livrakhah became a formula. When a Jew names someone who has died, he may add zikhrono livrakhah, "his memory for a blessing", written z"l; for a revered teacher, zekher tsaddiq livrakhah, written zt"l. The Mishnah already uses the verse to praise those who gave to the temple, and its second line for those who would not share their skills (Mishnah Yoma 3:11). In Israel's world a person lived on in his name and his children (Psalm 112:6; Isaiah 56:5), so for a name to "rot" was to be cut off for good.

a: a stubborn fool who keeps talking
p: Literally "a stubborn fool of lips": someone whose folly shows in nonstop talk.
b: Proverbs has several words for a fool. The 'evil, translated here "stubborn fool", is the one who will not be taught (see the note at 1:7). "Of lips" says where his folly lives: he talks instead of listening. The wise of heart "take in" commands; the fool's lips keep moving. The verb in the second line, yillavet, "is brought down, thrown down", is rare (only here, 10:10 and Hosea 4:14). The whole line returns as 10:10b.

a: One who winks an eye
p: In Proverbs a wink is a signal between people plotting harm, not a friendly joke.
b: Proverbs pictures the troublemaker who talks with his body, winking, shuffling his feet and pointing (6:13), and one who "narrows his eyes" is planning twisted things (16:30). The psalmist prays that those who hate him may not "wink at me" (Psalm 35:19). So the first line is a warning about secret signals and quiet plots, which cause pain. The second line repeats 10:8b. The Greek has a different second line, "but one who rebukes openly makes peace" (see the variant).

a: a spring of life
p: Living water in a dry land: Proverbs gives this picture to good speech, wise teaching and the fear of the LORD.
b: In a land that depends on rain and wells, a spring (maqor) that never stops is life itself. Proverbs calls four things a spring of life: the mouth of the righteous (here), the teaching of the wise (13:14), the fear of the LORD (14:27) and good sense (16:22); compare 18:4. The Psalms and the prophets give the image to God himself: "For with you is the spring of life" (Psalm 36:9), and Jeremiah calls the LORD "the spring of living water" that Israel left (Jeremiah 2:13; Jeremiah 17:13). Jesus' offer of water that "will become a spring inside him, of water leaping up into eternal life" (John 4:14) draws on the same picture.

a: love lays a cover over all wrongdoing
p: Two New Testament letters quote this line, and they follow the Hebrew, not the Greek.
b: To "cover" a wrong here is to forgive it and let it rest, not to hide a crime (compare 17:9, where covering an offense is a way of seeking love). Hatred digs up old wrongs and keeps the fight alive. The New Testament quotes the line twice: "love covers a crowd of sins" (1 Peter 4:8), and the one who brings back a straying brother "will cover a crowd of sins" (James 5:20). Both follow the Hebrew. The Greek of Proverbs has something else: "friendship covers all who do not love quarrels". So these writers knew a form of the saying closer to the Hebrew, or knew it as a common proverb. Paul's "love bears all things" (1 Corinthians 13:7) uses a verb that also means "covers".

a: for the back of the senseless there is a rod
p: The rod was a real stick for beating, used on fools who would not learn by words.
b: The shevet is a stick or rod: a shepherd's club, a ruler's scepter, and a tool for punishment. Proverbs sets it beside the back several times (19:29; 26:3). The contrast is between someone who learns from words, whose lips carry wisdom, and someone "lacking heart" (chasar lev, the senseless person of 6:32 and 7:7) who will only learn from pain. On the rod in raising children, see the notes at 13:24. In the Greek, Codex Vaticanus (as Swete prints it) has only the second line. Sinaiticus and Alexandrinus add the first and join the two into one sentence, "He who brings wisdom from his lips strikes the senseless man with a rod", and Rahlfs' edition prints that longer form.

a: A rich man's wealth is a fortress town to him;
p: This saying describes how the world works. A later saying adds that the rich man's walls are in his own imagination.
b: Many sayings in Proverbs simply observe: wealth protects and poverty ruins. That is true in any economy, and the saying makes no claim that it is good. The book checks the observation elsewhere: 18:10–11 sets "the name of the LORD", a strong tower, beside the rich man's walled town, "a high wall in his own imagination", and 11:4 says wealth is no help on the day of fury. Readers have to weigh sayings against each other; the sages expected that (see 26:4–5). The point is often a warning: the poor have no buffer, so oppressing them is crushing (14:31; 22:22–23).

a: goes toward sin
p: Chatta't means "sin", and sometimes the result of sin. Some versions translate "punishment".
b: The pair is "life" and chatta't. Most often the word means "sin", which makes the line say that the wicked use what they earn to do more wrong. Because "life" in the first line is an outcome, some translators give chatta't its sense of the penalty sin brings (as in Zechariah 14:19, "the punishment of Egypt"), and the Greek has "sins". The Plain keeps "sin". Either way, the saying looks at where a person's earnings lead.

a: sends people the wrong way
p: Mat'eh can mean "leads others astray" or "goes astray" himself. The Plain takes the first.
b: Mat'eh is a causative form of ta'ah, "to wander", and its usual sense is "leads astray" (as in Isaiah 3:12; Jeremiah 50:6). Read that way, the one who rejects rebuke harms others as well as himself, while the one who keeps discipline is "a path toward life" for others to walk. Some scholars and older versions take the form as inner-causative, "goes astray" or "errs": the person who will not be corrected loses his own way. Both readings fit the book; the Plain follows the usual sense of the verb form.

a: With many words, wrongdoing does not stop;
p: Talking too much is the path to wrongdoing: a teaching shared by Israel's sages, Egypt's and the rabbis.
b: The verb "does not stop" (lo yechdal) means the wrong never runs out where words pile up. The idea is everywhere in wisdom writing. Ecclesiastes warns, "let your words be few" (Ecclesiastes 5:2). The Mishnah gives Shimon son of Gamaliel the saying, "I have found nothing better for the body than silence... and whoever talks a lot brings on sin" (Mishnah Avot 1:17). James says that anyone who never stumbles in speech is a mature man (James 3:2) and that all should be "quick to hear, slow to speak" (James 1:19). Egyptian teachers praised "the silent man" in the same way.

a: Silver of the finest
t: Speech worth more than silver: Egypt
p: Egypt's Instruction of Ptahhotep also prizes good speech as a hidden treasure.
b: "Chosen" silver is refined, sorted metal. The Egyptian Instruction of Ptahhotep, copied in Middle Kingdom manuscripts (about 1900 BC), says "good speech is more hidden than greenstone, yet it may be found among maids at the grindstones" (translated in Lichtheim, vol. 1). Both teachers value speech above precious things, and both set it against what lies inside the wicked ("worth next to nothing"). The likeness is general: it shows a common outlook among the scribes of the ancient Near East, not that one text copied the other. Compare 8:19, where Wisdom's fruit is better than chosen silver.

a: shepherd many people
p: The verb is ra'ah, "to graze, shepherd". Good words feed people the way a shepherd leads a flock to pasture.
b: Ra'ah is a shepherd's verb: to pasture, to feed, to lead (Psalm 23:1, "The LORD is my shepherd", uses its participle). The righteous man's words nourish and guide many, while fools die "for lack of heart", that is, of sense. Proverbs uses the same verb for fools at 15:14: their mouths "graze on folly". The word also appears in 13:20, "one who keeps company with fools", where ro'eh means a companion.

a: and toil adds nothing to it.
p: The KJV reads "he adds no sorrow with it". The word order also allows "toil" as the subject: "toil adds nothing to it".
b: The word 'etsev means pain, sorrow and hard toil (the related word in Genesis 3:16–17 is the "pain" and "toil" of the curse). The word order allows 'etsev as the subject, and many modern translations take it that way: "toil does not add to it": what makes a person rich is the LORD's blessing, and anxious labor adds nothing beyond it. Psalm 127:2 says much the same ("eating bread earned with pain"). The older reading makes the LORD the subject: he gives wealth with no sorrow attached. Neither reading says work is useless (10:4 has just praised hard work); they say the outcome is the LORD's. The verse is sometimes used to promise wealth to the faithful, but Proverbs also says a little with the fear of the LORD is better than great treasure (15:16).

a: doing something vile
p: Zimmah is a shameful scheme, in the Law most often a sexual one. The fool does it for fun.
b: Zimmah comes from zamam, "to plan", like mezimmah (1:4), but it nearly always means a wicked plan (at Job 17:11 it means simply "my plans"), and in the Law it is used for sexual crimes such as incest (Leviticus 18:17; Leviticus 20:14). The fool treats such things as a game, "like laughter" (kischoq). The second line is short and has no verb, so it borrows from the first: wisdom is the same kind of delight for a person of understanding. The Greek reads it differently: "wisdom gives birth to good sense for a man".

a: When the storm passes
p: A storm sweeps the wicked away; the righteous stand like a foundation. Jesus told the same story about two builders.
b: Sufah is a whirlwind or gale, the kind of storm that strips a field (Job 21:18; Psalm 83:15). The righteous are "a foundation of forever": the picture is of a building that stays when the wind has passed. Jesus ends the Sermon on the Mount with the same contrast: the house built on rock stands through the storm, and the one built on sand falls (Matthew 7:24–27). The rabbis read the verse of the righteous person as the foundation on which the world stands (Bavli Chagigah 12b).

a: The fear of the LORD adds days,
t: Long life: a promise or a rule of thumb?
p: Proverbs links goodness with long life; Job and Ecclesiastes know of righteous people who die young.
b: For "the fear of the LORD", see the note at 1:7. Proverbs often says the righteous live long and the wicked die early (3:2, 16; 9:11; 10:27; 14:27). Read alone, that sounds like a guarantee. Other wisdom books push back: Job asks why the wicked "reach old age" (Job 21:7), and Ecclesiastes has seen "a righteous man who dies in his righteousness" (Ecclesiastes 7:15). Most interpreters, Jewish and Christian, take the sayings as what usually happens under God's rule, the way of the world when things go as they should, not a promise for every case. Others read them as finally true beyond this life (see the note at 12:28). The Bible holds both voices.

a: the wicked will not stay settled in the land.
p: The promise of living on in the land runs from Deuteronomy through Psalm 37 to Jesus' "they will inherit the earth".
b: Erets can mean "the land" (of Israel) or "the earth". In Deuteronomy, staying in the land is the reward of keeping the covenant (Deuteronomy 4:40; Deuteronomy 25:15), and Proverbs uses the same language in its own way (2:21–22). Psalm 37 repeats it: "But the humble will take possession of the land / and delight in great peace" (Psalm 37:11). Jesus' saying "Blessed are the gentle, because they will inherit the earth" (Matthew 5:5) quotes that psalm, and Christian readers have read the promise as a new earth (Revelation 21:1).

a: bears wisdom as its fruit
p: The verb nuv means "to sprout, bear fruit". The mouth is pictured as a tree, and a twisted tongue as a branch cut off.
b: Yanuv is a plant word (compare Psalm 92:14, "In old age they will still yield fruit"). The righteous man's mouth grows wisdom like fruit. The second line keeps the picture: a tongue "of twistings" (tahpukhot, a word for perverse, upside-down talk, also 10:32; 2:12) will be "cut off", the verb for cutting down a tree or pruning a branch. The image of speech as fruit runs through these chapters (12:14; 13:2; 18:20–21).

a: Scales that cheat are abhorrent to the LORD,
p: Buying and selling meant weighing silver on a balance with stone weights, and a dishonest merchant kept two sets.
b: Before coins, silver was weighed. A trader hung a balance (mo'zenayim, "the pair of scales") and set carved stones ('even, "stone") in one pan; archaeologists have found many such weights in Judah, inscribed with the shekel sign and numbers. A cheat used a heavy stone to buy and a light one to sell. The Law forbids it: "Do not keep two kinds of weights in your bag, a heavy one and a light one" (Deuteronomy 25:13), and the prophets condemn it (Amos 8:5; Micah 6:11). Egypt's Instruction of Amenemope has the same rule: "Do not move the scales nor alter the weights" (chapter 16). "Abhorrent" (to'evah) is the strongest word Proverbs has for what the LORD hates; the full, true weight, a "whole stone", "wins his favor". The saying recurs in 16:11; 20:10, 23.

a: In comes arrogance, and in comes shame;
t: Pride and shame, with a rhyme
p: Zadon and qalon rhyme. The word for "modest" appears elsewhere only in Micah 6:8.
b: The line runs "comes zadon, and comes qalon": arrogance arrives, and shame follows on its heels. The Plain keeps the repeated "in comes". Tsenu'im, "the modest", is rare; its verb is in Micah's "walk humbly (or modestly) with your God" (Micah 6:8). In later Hebrew tseni'ut is the word for modesty in dress and behavior. The familiar "Pride goes before a fall" is a different saying, 16:18; this one says that shame, not only a fall, comes with pride.

a: Wealth is no help on the day of fury,
t: A verse missing from most of the Greek
p: The second line repeats 10:2b. Codices Vaticanus and Sinaiticus lack the verse, and Rahlfs does not print it.
b: "The day of fury" is the day God's anger breaks out, a phrase the prophets use for the day of the LORD: "Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to save them on the day of the LORD's fury" (Zephaniah 1:18; compare Ezekiel 7:19). Proverbs applies it to any day of disaster or judgment. The second line is word for word 10:2b (see the note there). In the Greek, Codex Vaticanus (the main text in Swete's edition) and Codex Sinaiticus pass from 11:3 to 11:5, and Rahlfs' edition does not print the verse. Codex Alexandrinus has a Greek form of it, together with a line close to the Hebrew 11:3 (Swete's apparatus). The Hebrew manuscripts all have it.
orig: לֹא־יוֹעִיל הוֹן בְּיוֹם עֶבְרָה (lo-yo'il hon beyom 'evrah)

a: the wicked man takes his place in it.
p: Haman hanged on the pole he set up for Mordecai is the Bible's most famous case of this saying.
b: The pattern of the trap that catches its maker runs through the Bible's stories. Haman is impaled on the pole he set up for Mordecai (Esther 7:9–10); the men who accused Daniel are thrown to the lions in his place (Daniel 6:24). 21:18 says it again: "the wicked are a ransom for the righteous". The saying does not explain how this works; it states it as the way God's world runs (compare Psalm 7:15–16).

a: A godless man
p: The KJV's "hypocrite" comes from the Greek and Latin of a later age. Chanef means someone polluted, godless.
b: Chanef comes from a verb meaning "to be defiled": the land is "polluted" by blood (Numbers 35:33). A chanef is a person with no regard for God (Job 8:13: "the godless man's hope will be lost"). The KJV's "hypocrite" follows later Jewish and Greek usage, which took the word as "pretender", and that sense colored the English Bible. Here the godless man uses his mouth to ruin his neighbor: slander, lies or false testimony. The righteous get free "through knowledge": they see through it.

a: A town celebrates when the righteous prosper,
p: Proverbs pictures the town as a whole: it rises or falls with the kind of people who lead it.
b: Verses 10–11 move from the household to the qiryah, the town: its people cheer when the righteous do well and when the wicked are gone, and its fate rides on what is said in it, blessing or slander. The same thought comes back in later sayings about rulers (28:12, 28; 29:2). In Codex Vaticanus of the Greek, 11:10b and 11:11a are missing, so the verse reads "In the good of the righteous a city prospered, but by the mouths of the ungodly it was dug up"; a later corrector of Vaticanus added the missing lines in the margin, and Alexandrinus and a corrector of Sinaiticus have them (Swete's apparatus). Rahlfs' edition prints the shorter text.

a: One who goes around telling tales
p: Rakhil, a gossip who goes from house to house, is the word of Leviticus 19:16.
b: Holekh rakhil, "one who goes about as a talebearer", is the phrase of the Law: "Do not go about as a slanderer among your kin" (Leviticus 19:16). The sod he lays bare is a confidence, the private counsel of friends or of a ruler's circle. The opposite is "a faithful spirit", a person you can trust with a secret. 20:19 repeats the first line and draws the lesson: do not mix with a blabbermouth. The rabbis built on these verses their teaching on lashon hara, harmful talk about others.

a: Where no one steers
p: Tachbulot, "guidance", is a sailor's word: the skill of the man at the ropes.
b: Tachbulot is related to chevel, "rope", and chovel, "sailor" (the ship's captain in Jonah 1:6 is the rav hachovel, "chief of the sailors"). The image is of a ship steered by a skilled hand. A people without such steering falls; with many advisers there is "rescue" (teshu'ah, the word also used for victory in battle). The same advice is given for war in 20:18 and 24:6, and for plans in 15:22. The word first appears in 1:5, where the person of understanding "acquires steering".

a: Stand good for an outsider's loan
p: Proverbs warns again and again against guaranteeing someone else's debt.
b: To stand surety ('arav) was to promise to pay another person's debt if he did not, sealed with a handshake, "striking hands" (toq'im). If the borrower failed, the guarantor lost his goods, even his bed (22:26–27). The warning comes many times (6:1–5; 17:18; 20:16; 22:26–27; 27:13). Here the borrower is a zar, an outsider to the family, someone you cannot hold to account. Judah, out of love, tells his father "I will be his guarantor" for Benjamin (Genesis 43:9), and the later sage Ben Sira is warmer: "A good man will be surety for his neighbor" (Sirach 29:14). The Plain gives the Hebrew's "harm, he will be harmed" as "badly hurt".

a: A woman of grace takes hold of honor,
t: A gracious woman, and the ruthless
p: The second line may contrast with the first or compare to it. The Greek adds two lines.
b: The verb "take hold of" (tamakh) is the same in both lines. Either the saying contrasts the woman who gains honor by grace with ruthless men who gain only wealth, or it compares them: as surely as the ruthless get rich, a gracious woman wins honor. The Hebrew "and" allows both, and the Plain keeps "and". The ruthless ('aritsim) are tyrants and bullies (Job 6:23; Psalm 54:3). The Greek turns the verse into four lines: a gracious wife raises up glory for her husband, a woman who hates what is right is a throne of dishonor, the lazy lack wealth, and the hard-working prop themselves up with wealth (see the variant). Proverbs later warns that "grace" can be false (31:30).

a: stirs up trouble for his own flesh
p: The verb 'akhar is the word Joshua used to Achan, and it names the Valley of Achor.
b: 'Okher, "one who stirs up trouble", is a strong verb, used of bringing disaster on a family or a people. Joshua says to Achan, "Why have you brought trouble on us? The LORD will bring trouble on you this day" (Joshua 7:25), and the place is named the Valley of Achor, "Trouble" (Joshua 7:26). Proverbs uses it three times in these chapters: the cruel man troubles "his own flesh" (she'er, his body or his blood relatives), the fool troubles his own house (11:29), and so does the greedy man (15:27). The opposite is the ish chesed, "a person of loyal love", who does good to his own nefesh, his very self.

a: pay that turns out fake
p: The Hebrew plays on sheqer, "falsehood", and seker, "wages".
b: The wicked man earns "wages of sheqer" (falsehood); the one who sows righteousness earns "seker of truth". The two words sound almost the same. Wicked gain is false: it looks like profit and then vanishes (compare 13:11; 21:6). The Plain tries to keep the sound with "fake" and "real". Paul uses the sowing image the same way (Galatians 6:7–9; Hosea 10:12).

a: Firm righteousness
p: The first word, ken, usually means "so", but can also mean "firm, true". The Greek read ben, "son".
b: The verse begins ken-tsedaqah. If ken is the common word "so" or "thus", the verse is linked to the one before ("So righteousness leads to life"). It can also be an adjective, "firm, honest" (as in Genesis 42:11, "honest men"), which gives "Firm righteousness" or "One who is firm in righteousness". The Plain takes this second reading. The Greek has "A righteous son is born for life", reading ben, "son", for ken; the two letters look alike in Hebrew script. "Heads for his own death" is literally "is for his death".

a: You can shake hands on it:
p: Yad leyad, "hand to hand", is a pledge: as sure as a handshake. The KJV read it as wicked people joining hands.
b: The phrase is a gesture of assurance, like striking hands on a deal (11:15; 17:18). So the line means "Be sure of it: the evil man will not go unpunished" (literally "will not be held innocent", lo yinnaqeh, a legal verb). The KJV's "Though hand join in hand, the wicked shall not be unpunished" takes it as conspirators linking hands; most scholars now take it as an oath-like "you can count on it". The same phrase opens 16:5b. "The children" is literally "the seed", the descendants of the righteous.

a: A gold ring in a pig's snout:
p: A nose ring was fine jewelry. On a pig, an unclean animal rooting in filth, beauty is wasted.
b: Women wore gold nose rings (nezem) as jewelry and as bridal gifts: "So I put the ring on her nose" (Genesis 24:47; compare Isaiah 3:21; Ezekiel 16:12). The pig was unclean for Israel (Leviticus 11:7) and roots in mud, so the picture is grotesque on purpose. The woman has "turned away from ta'am": taste, judgment, good sense. The same word is used of Abigail, whom David praises: "blessed is your clear thinking" (1 Samuel 25:33). The saying is addressed to young men choosing a wife, and like 31:30 it puts character above looks. Modern readers notice that Proverbs says this of women only; a saying about a handsome man without sense would carry the same truth.
orig: נֶזֶם זָהָב בְּאַף חֲזִיר (nezem zahav be'af chazir)

a: Someone scatters freely, and he ends up with still more;
p: Scattering, like a farmer sowing seed, brings more. Paul builds on the same idea in 2 Corinthians 9.
b: Mefazzer is "one who scatters", like seed or gifts to the poor: "He has scattered, he has given to the needy" (Psalm 112:9). The one who holds back "from what is right" (miyyosher: more than is right, or what it is right to give) ends up in want. Verses 24–26 make a little group on generosity and hoarding. Paul uses the farmer's logic for the collection for Jerusalem: "The one who sows sparingly will also reap sparingly" (2 Corinthians 9:6), and he quotes Psalm 112:9 a few lines later (2 Corinthians 9:9). Compare Ecclesiastes 11:1–2.

a: The one who hoards grain, people curse,
p: In a bad year a man with full barns could hold back grain until prices rose. The verb for selling is used of Joseph.
b: Mashbir, "one who sells grain", is the word used of Joseph in Egypt: "he was the one selling grain to all its people" (Genesis 42:6). In a famine a landowner could keep his stores off the market to drive the price up. The people's curse on him was not just anger: a curse was a serious appeal to God. Amos condemns the merchants who cannot wait for the Sabbath to end so they can sell grain with false measures (Amos 8:5–6). The saying praises the one who sells, not the one who gives: fair trade in hard times is itself a blessing.

a: a slave to the one with a wise heart
p: Eved means a servant or a slave by context. A fool who wrecked his household might end up working off his debts.
b: 'Eved covers everyone who works for a master: the king's ministers are his "servants" (14:35), and a person sold for debt is a "slave". The site translates by context. Here the fool who has brought ruin on his own house inherits "wind", nothing at all, and may end up as a bondservant to a wise man; Israel's law allowed a debtor to work off what he owed (Exodus 21:2–6; Leviticus 25:39–43; 2 Kings 4:1). In 17:2 a wise slave even takes a share of the family inheritance over a disgraceful son. The 1955 play Inherit the Wind took its title from this verse.

a: a tree of life
p: The tree of Eden returns in Proverbs as an everyday picture of what gives life.
b: In Genesis the LORD God plants "the tree of life in the middle of the garden" (Genesis 2:9), and the way back to it is closed after the fall (Genesis 3:22–24). Proverbs uses the phrase four times, always for something in reach: Wisdom herself (3:18), the fruit of the righteous (here), a longing fulfilled (13:12), and a healing tongue (15:4). For the sages, the life Eden lost can be tasted again in wise and good living. Revelation brings the tree back for good: "On each side of the river stood the tree of life" (Revelation 22:2; compare Revelation 2:7).

a: and one who wins people over is wise.
p: The KJV's "he that winneth souls is wise" became a motto for evangelism. The Hebrew is harder.
b: Loqeach nefashot literally means "one who takes lives", and elsewhere it means killing (1 Kings 19:4; Psalm 31:13). Nefesh here means a person or a life, not the soul in the later sense. Readers have taken the line three ways: the wise man "captures" people, winning them over with his good fruit (the Plain, close to the KJV); the wise man saves lives (the choice of several modern versions); or a letter has been miscopied, and the original was "violence (chamas) takes lives", a contrast with the first line, as the Greek's "the lives of the lawless are taken away before their time" suggests (see the variant). Charles Spurgeon opened his book The Soul Winner (1895) with the KJV reading, and "soul winning" became a common phrase in evangelical churches.

a: how much more the wicked man and the sinner!
t: Quoted in 1 Peter from the Greek
p: The Hebrew says the righteous are repaid on earth; the Greek says "barely saved". 1 Peter 4:18 quotes the Greek.
b: The Hebrew argues from the lesser to the greater: if even the righteous get what they deserve in this life (for their faults as well as their good), the wicked surely will. The Greek of Proverbs reads: "If the righteous is barely saved, where will the ungodly and sinner appear?" (checked in Swete's edition of Codex Vaticanus). 1 Peter 4:18 quotes this Greek exactly: "If the righteous person is saved only with difficulty, where will the ungodly and the sinner show up?" Peter is writing to churches facing suffering, and he reads the line as a word about the last judgment, which "begins with the household of God" (1 Peter 4:17). The two forms agree on the main point, that judgment touches the righteous first and the wicked worst. See the variant.

a: as dumb as an animal
p: Ba'ar comes from the word for cattle. One who hates correction has the mind of a farm animal.
b: Ba'ar is related to be'ir, "livestock". The KJV's "brutish" keeps the picture. The psalmist uses it of himself: "I was stupid; I knew nothing. / I was a dumb animal with you" (Psalm 73:22), and Agur says, "I am more beast than man" (30:2). An animal cannot be taught by words, only steered by force; a person who hates rebuke chooses to be like that. Compare Psalm 32:9.

a: A woman of strength is her husband's crown,
p: 'Eshet chayil, the phrase of the closing poem (31:10) and of Boaz's words to Ruth.
b: Chayil means strength, ability, wealth and worth; it is the word for an army and for a "mighty man of valor". The 'eshet chayil appears again in 31:10, where the closing poem describes her at length, and in Ruth 3:11, where Boaz tells Ruth that "the whole town knows that you are a woman of worth" (the same Hebrew, 'eshet chayil; in Ruth this site keeps "a woman of worth" on purpose, to pair her with Boaz, "a man of great worth", Ruth 2:1). A crown ('ateret) is honor that others can see. The wife who brings shame (mevishah, the same word used of the son in 10:5) is "like rot in his bones", a hidden, wasting disease (compare 14:30). The saying looks at marriage from the husband's side, because the sayings were first spoken to young men; it still makes the wife the source of the household's honor.

a: the mouth of the upright gets them out
p: "Them" may be the upright themselves or the victims the wicked lie in wait for.
b: The first line pictures the words of the wicked as an ambush "for blood": lying testimony, a plot, slander that could get someone killed (1:11, 18). In the second line "them" has no clear antecedent. It may be the upright, whose own words save them from the trap, or the innocent people the wicked are hunting, whom the upright rescue by speaking up, perhaps in court. Either way, the mouth is a weapon in one line and a rescue in the other.

a: A righteous man knows what his animal needs,
p: The righteous "know the nefesh" of their animals: their life and needs. Jewish law built a principle on such texts.
b: Nefesh is life, appetite and inner self, the same word used of people. The righteous man knows what his animal feels and needs. The Law commands rest for working animals on the Sabbath (Exodus 23:12; Deuteronomy 5:14), help for a fallen donkey (Exodus 23:5; Deuteronomy 22:4), and an unmuzzled ox at the threshing floor (Deuteronomy 25:4). The rabbis drew from these laws the principle of tsa'ar ba'alei chayyim, avoiding the suffering of living creatures (Bavli Bava Metzia 32b), and later writers cite this verse alongside them. God's own care for animals ends the book of Jonah (Jonah 4:11). The second line is sharp: even the wicked's "compassion" (rachamim) is cruel.
r: Exodus 23:5; Exodus 23:12; Deuteronomy 22:4; Deuteronomy 25:4; Jonah 4:11; Psalm 145:9; Luke 12:6

a: the man who chases empty things
p: Reqim can mean empty schemes or empty, worthless men. The Greek adds a couplet about wine.
b: Reqim means "empty ones": worthless pursuits, or worthless men, as in Judges 9:4 and 11:3, where Abimelech and Jephthah gather "empty men". The farmer who works his own land eats; the one who chases get-rich schemes or bad company has no sense (chasar lev). 28:19 repeats the first line and ends with poverty. The Greek adds a couplet: "Whoever is pleasant in the pastimes of wine will leave dishonor in his own strongholds."

a: The wicked covet what evil men catch in their nets,
p: The Hebrew is very hard. Scholars have proposed many readings, and none has won.
b: Word for word the line says, "The wicked covets the net (or stronghold) of evil men, and the root of the righteous gives." Metsod can mean a hunting net, its catch, or a fortress. The second line needs an object ("gives fruit"). The Plain takes the plainest sense: the wicked envy what other crooks have caught, while the righteous have a root that produces on its own. The Greek has "The desires of the ungodly are evil, but the roots of the godly are in strongholds", and many scholars change a word or two to get a better contrast. Translations differ widely here.
orig: חָמַד רָשָׁע מְצוֹד רָעִים (chamad rasha' metsod ra'im)

a: A man is filled with good from the fruit his mouth bears,
p: Words are like a tree's fruit: a person eats what his own mouth produces.
b: Proverbs pictures speech as a crop. A man is filled with the good his words produce (here), eats the good from it (13:2), and "A man fills his belly with what his mouth bears" (18:20); "Death and life are in the tongue's hand" (18:21). Jesus uses the same picture: a tree is known by its fruit, and "It is by your words that you will be justified" (Matthew 12:33–37). The second line widens it from words to deeds: what the hands do comes back. On the reading "is paid back", see the variant.

a: the shrewd man keeps an insult covered
p: 'Arum is the word for the serpent in Genesis 3:1. In Proverbs it is a virtue: thinking ahead.
b: 'Arum, "shrewd", has a good sense in Proverbs (see the note at 1:4): the shrewd person thinks before acting and plans ahead (13:16; 14:8, 15, 18; 22:3). The same word describes the serpent in Genesis 3:1 as "crafty", the bad side of the same skill. Here shrewdness means self-control. The fool's anger is known "that day", at once; the shrewd man "covers" (kosseh) the insult (qalon, shame or disgrace done to him), letting it pass, like the love that covers in 10:12.

a: One who breathes out the truth
p: Many of these sayings are about testimony at the town gate, where a lying witness could cost a life.
b: Israel's courts met at the town gate, and verdicts depended on witnesses (Deuteronomy 19:15). The Ten Words forbid false testimony: "You must not testify against your neighbor as a lying witness" (Exodus 20:16), and a witness caught lying received the penalty he had meant for the accused (Deuteronomy 19:16–19). The verb yafiach, "breathes out", is used in Proverbs almost only of witnesses (6:19; 14:5, 25; 19:5, 9), and some scholars think a noun from the same root meant "witness" (compare Psalm 27:12). These chapters return to the honest and the lying witness again and again (12:19; 14:5, 25).

a: words that stab like a sword
p: Thoughtless words stab; wise words heal. The image runs from the Psalms to James and Ben Sira.
b: Boteh is someone who speaks rashly, blurting without thinking (as in Leviticus 5:4, a thoughtless oath; Psalm 106:33). His words are "like the thrusts of a sword". The Psalms speak of tongues sharpened like swords (Psalm 57:4; Psalm 64:3). James calls the tongue a fire (James 3:6), and Ben Sira says that many have fallen by the edge of the sword, but not as many as have fallen because of the tongue (Sirach 28:18). The "tongue of the wise" is a marpe', a cure, the same word as in 13:17; 14:30; 15:4.

a: Those who plow up evil
p: Charash means both "to plow" and "to plan". Evil is plowed and planted like a field.
b: Choreshe ra' are "plowers of evil". The verb charash is used for plowing a field and for working metal, and so for planning or devising (3:29; 6:14, 18). The farm picture fits a book that speaks of sowing and reaping (11:18; 22:8); Hosea says, "You plowed wickedness. You harvested injustice" (Hosea 10:13, in fresh wording). 14:22 uses the same word for those who "plow up good".

a: No trouble at all will fall to the righteous man,
p: Read as a guarantee, this verse would be false. Psalm 34:19 says the opposite about the righteous.
b: The saying is absolute: "Not any trouble will happen to the righteous." Yet the Psalms say, "Many are the evils that strike a righteous person, / but out of all of them the LORD rescues him" (Psalm 34:19), and Job is the Bible's long argument that the righteous do suffer. Proverbs itself knows that the righteous fall seven times and get up (24:16). Most readers take sayings like this as general truths stated without exceptions, the way a proverb works in any language ("Haste makes waste"). Some Jewish and Christian interpreters read them as finally true: whatever happens, no harm can touch the righteous in the end (compare Romans 8:28). See also the note at 10:27.

a: a slack hand will end up doing forced labor
p: Mas is the labor gang a king drafted. Solomon used it to build the temple and his palaces.
b: Mas is forced labor, work owed to the king. "King Solomon drafted a labor force out of all Israel" (1 Kings 5:13), and the burden of it split the kingdom: Israel stoned "Adoram, the man over the forced labor" (1 Kings 12:18). The saying is a sharp one to put under Solomon's name: the hard workers will rule, and the slack will end up drafted for others' building projects. Compare the Canaanites put to forced labor in Joshua 16:10 and Judges 1:28.

a: A righteous man scouts out the road for his friend,
p: Yater may mean "guides", "scouts out" or "is better than". Translations go several ways.
b: Yater could come from tur, "to explore, scout" (as the spies "scouted" Canaan, Numbers 13:2), giving "the righteous scouts out (the way) for his friend" or "chooses his friends with care". Or it comes from yatar, "to be more", which the KJV took: "The righteous is more excellent than his neighbour." Some scholars change a letter and read "the righteous is delivered from harm". The Plain takes the scouting sense, which makes a contrast with the wicked, whose road "sends them wandering".

a: Slackness never gets its catch to the roasting fire,
p: The verb charakh appears only here. It probably means "to roast" or "to start" the game.
b: Yacharokh is found only here; in Aramaic the root means to singe or roast. So the lazy hunter either never roasts what he caught, or never "starts" game at all. Either way, his effort comes to nothing. The second line has puzzling word order ("wealth of a man, precious, diligent"); it probably means that a diligent man gains precious wealth, or that diligence is a man's precious wealth. The lazy one who buries his hand in the dish and will not bring it to his mouth (19:24; 26:15) is the same sort of humor.

a: and where its path goes, death is not.
p: The Hebrew 'al-mavet, "not death", may be the clearest hint in Proverbs of life that outlasts death.
b: Most of Proverbs speaks of life and death in this world: a long, full life or an early grave. This line is unusual. The Masoretic Text reads 'al-mavet, "no death", as if the road of righteousness leads to a life death cannot end. Some scholars (Mitchell Dahood, Bruce Waltke) take it that way, as a hint of immortality like Psalm 16:10–11 and Psalm 49:15. Others note that 'al normally negates a verb, not a noun, and with a change of vowels read 'el-mavet, "to death", which gives the usual contrast; the Greek has "to death" (see the variant). The Plain follows the Hebrew as it stands. Christian readers have long heard it in the light of John 8:51.

a: A father's discipline: a wise son takes it in;
p: The Hebrew says only "A wise son, a father's discipline". The verb has to be supplied.
b: The first line has no verb: ben chakham musar av, "a wise son, a father's discipline". Translators supply one: the son "hears" it (borrowing shama' from the second line, as the KJV does), "loves" it (a common emendation), or the son "is the product of" a father's discipline. The Plain keeps the gap close to the Hebrew and supplies "takes it in". The mocker (lets, see the note at 1:22) "does not listen to a scolding". The same words, lo shama' ge'arah, return in 13:8 with another meaning. Egypt's Ptahhotep ends his teaching with praise of "a son who hears".
orig: בֵּן חָכָם מוּסַר אָב (ben chakham musar av)

a: makes a stink
p: Hiv'ish means "to make something smell". It is Jacob's word to Simeon and Levi.
b: Yav'ish is from ba'ash, "to stink". Jacob uses it after the massacre at Shechem: "You have made me stink among the people of the land" (Genesis 34:30), and Saul's attack makes Israel "stink" to the Philistines (1 Samuel 13:4). So the wicked man makes himself and others hateful. The next verb, yachpir, "brings disgrace", sounds a little like it. Some translators read the pair as "acts shamefully and disgracefully"; others as "brings shame and disgrace" on others.

a: Righteousness stands guard over the one whose way has integrity,
t: A verse missing from Codex Vaticanus
p: Codices Vaticanus and Sinaiticus lack this verse; Alexandrinus has a version of it, and Rahlfs prints it.
b: The verse personifies righteousness as a guard and wickedness as the one who trips up the sinner. The Hebrew uses abstract nouns: "integrity of way" for the person of integrity and "sin" for the sinner. In the Greek, Codex Vaticanus and Codex Sinaiticus pass from 13:5 to 13:7; Codex Alexandrinus adds after 13:5 "Righteousness guards the innocent in the way, but sin makes the ungodly worthless" (Swete's apparatus), and Rahlfs' edition prints that verse. The Hebrew manuscripts have the verse. Fragments of chapters 13–15 survive in the Dead Sea Scroll 4QProv-b; as reported by its editors, its text is close to the Masoretic Text in what survives (see the chapter page).

a: One person acts rich and has nothing at all;
p: The verbs can mean "pretend to be rich" and "pretend to be poor", or "make oneself rich" and "make oneself poor".
b: Mit'asher and mitroshesh are reflexive forms. Most read them as pretending: one man puts on a show of wealth and has nothing; another hides great wealth behind a poor man's life. Others read them as doing: one man grasps at wealth and ends with nothing, another gives his wealth away and is truly rich, a paradox like 11:24. Paul describes his ministry "as poor, yet making many rich; as having nothing, and yet possessing everything" (2 Corinthians 6:10), and the risen Christ tells the church at Laodicea that its claim to be rich hides its poverty (Revelation 3:17).
orig: יֵשׁ מִתְעַשֵּׁר וְאֵין כֹּל (yesh mit'asher ve'en kol)

a: the poor man never even hears the threat
p: A rich man may have to pay a ransom for his life. No one bothers to threaten the poor.
b: Kofer is a ransom, the price paid for a life (Exodus 21:30: "he must pay whatever is set for him as the price of his life"). Wealth can buy a man out of danger, but it also makes him a target for kidnappers, blackmailers and corrupt officials. The poor man "does not hear a ge'arah": nobody bothers to threaten him. The four Hebrew words are the same as 13:1b, where they mean the mocker does not listen to a scolding. The repeat looks deliberate, a play on two senses of ge'arah, rebuke and threat.

a: the lamp of the wicked will go out
p: A burning lamp is a living household. A lamp that goes out is a family line ended.
b: A small clay oil lamp burned through the night in an Israelite house; a dark house was an empty one. So the lamp stands for life and for a line of descendants: David's men tell him, "Do not snuff out Israel's lamp" (2 Samuel 21:17), and God keeps "a lamp" for David in Jerusalem (1 Kings 11:36). Bildad says, "the wicked man's light is snuffed" (Job 18:5). The same line returns at 24:20, and 20:20 uses it of one who curses his parents. The light of the righteous "burns cheerfully" (literally "rejoices"). The Greek adds a couplet: "Deceitful souls go astray in sins, but the righteous have pity and show mercy."

a: Wealth that comes out of thin air
t: Wealth from a puff of air
p: Mehevel means "from hevel", the vapor of Ecclesiastes. The Greek reads "wealth hastened with lawlessness".
b: Hevel is breath or vapor, the word Ecclesiastes uses for everything that vanishes. Wealth "from hevel" is money that comes from nothing: easy gain, speculation, a fraud. The contrast is the one who gathers "on the hand", that is, by hand, bit by bit, by his own work. The Greek has "wealth hastened with lawlessness", as if its Hebrew read mevohal, "hurried" (compare 20:21; 28:20). Several modern versions follow that. The Plain keeps the Hebrew, which makes good sense as it stands.

a: One who scorns a word will be bound to pay for it,
p: The verb may mean "be held to a pledge" or "be ruined". The rabbis read "word" as the word of God.
b: Yechavel lo may come from chaval I, "to take a pledge": the one who despises an instruction becomes its debtor and has to pay. Or it comes from chaval II, "to ruin": he ruins himself. "Word" and "command" (mitsvah) are parallel. The sages may mean a parent's or teacher's instruction (as in 13:14), but Jewish and Christian readers have often taken them as the word of God. The Greek adds a long couplet: "A deceitful son will have nothing good, but a wise servant's deeds will prosper, and his way will be made straight."
orig: בָּז לְדָבָר יֵחָבֶל לוֹ (baz ledavar yechavel lo)

a: The teaching of the wise
p: This site renders torah "law", but here the context forces "teaching": the instruction of a wise teacher.
b: Across the Bible this site translates torah "law". In Proverbs, though, torah is usually the teaching of a parent or a sage (1:8; 3:1; 4:2; 6:20, 23; 7:2), and "the law of the wise" would mislead a modern reader, so the Plain has "teaching" (see the note at 1:8). The line is almost the same as 14:27, where "the fear of the LORD" takes the place of "the teaching of the wise": the sages saw the two as one source of life. Later Jewish tradition heard all of these as the Torah of Moses, and the Greek translates "law" (nomos).

a: hard as rock
p: 'Eitan usually means "lasting, ever-flowing". The KJV made it "hard". The Greek has "in ruin".
b: 'Eitan describes what is permanent: a stream that never dries (Amos 5:24) or an enduring nation (Jeremiah 5:15). "The road of the treacherous is lasting" makes little sense, so the KJV took it as "hard", like rock that does not change (compare Numbers 24:21), and the Plain follows that. Many scholars think a word dropped out ("is not lasting"), or follow the Greek, which reads "the ways of the scornful lead to ruin" (see the variant). The Greek also adds a line: "to know the law belongs to a good mind".

a: one who keeps company with fools comes to grief
p: Ro'eh and yeroa' sound alike: a companion of fools will be harmed.
b: The second line plays on sound: ro'eh kesilim yeroa', "a companion of fools will be harmed". Ro'eh is a friend or someone who grazes with you (see the note at 10:21); yeroa' means "will suffer harm". The first line has a marginal reading: the written text has commands, "Walk with the wise and become wise"; the reading the Masoretes said aloud has "One who walks... will grow wise" (see the variant). Paul quotes a Greek proverb with the same idea: "Bad company ruins good character" (1 Corinthians 15:33).

a: stored away for the righteous
p: The idea that the wicked pile up wealth for the righteous to inherit appears in Job and Ecclesiastes too.
b: The verse has two halves. A good man's inheritance reaches his grandchildren: in Israel, family land (nachalah) was meant to stay in the family for good. The wicked man's wealth, by contrast, does not last in his line; it ends up with the righteous. Job says the wicked may heap up silver, "a righteous man wears it" (Job 27:16–17), and Ecclesiastes says God gives the sinner the work of gathering for the one who pleases God (Ecclesiastes 2:26). Some modern preachers teach a coming "wealth transfer" to believers from this verse; most commentators read it as a statement about how ill-gotten gain fails to last, not a program.

a: but some are swept away where there is no justice.
p: The Hebrew is hard. It seems to say that the poor can grow food, but injustice can sweep them away.
b: Nir is newly broken or fallow ground. Rashim are "poor people", spelled here with an aleph like ra'shim, "heads" or "chiefs". "There is one swept away (nispeh) for lack of justice" may refer to the poor themselves or to their crops. The likely sense: even a poor family's small plot can feed them, if no one robs them through crooked courts or land grabs. The verse is one of the few in Proverbs that blames poverty on injustice rather than laziness (compare 14:31; 22:22–23). The Greek has a different verse: "The righteous will spend many years in wealth, but the unrighteous will perish quickly."

a: keeps back his rod
t: The rod, and a line that is not in the Bible
p: Shevet is a real rod, used for beating. "Spare the rod and spoil the child" is not a Bible verse.
b: Shevet is a stick or staff: the shepherd's club of Psalm 23:4 ("Your club and your staff, they reassure me"), a ruler's scepter, and the rod used to punish (10:13; 22:15; 23:13–14; 26:3; 29:15). God's promise to David's son uses it: "I will correct him with a rod such as men use" (2 Samuel 7:14). Here it means physical punishment, and the Plain keeps "rod". Chosekh, "keeps back", is the verb of 10:19 (holding back the lips) and 11:24 (holding back what is fair to give). The familiar "Spare the rod and spoil the child" is best known in this form from Samuel Butler's comic poem Hudibras (1664), where it is used of love-making, not child rearing. The proverb itself is older: Langland's Piers Plowman (late 1300s) has "Who-so spareth the sprynge spilleth his children". The Greek has "staff" (baktēria).

a: hates his son
t: How Jews and Christians read the rod today
p: Many Jewish and Christian teachers now stress loving discipline without hitting; others defend physical punishment.
b: In Hebrew idiom "hate" can mean "love less" or "reject" (Genesis 29:31; Deuteronomy 21:15), but here the point is blunt: a parent who never corrects a child is acting against the child's good. Modern readers divide over the means. In Jewish life, the Talmud's limits are often cited: strike a pupil only with a light strap (Bavli Bava Batra 21a), never a grown son (Bavli Moed Katan 17a), and let "the left hand push away while the right hand draws near" (Bavli Sotah 47a). In 2000 Israel's Supreme Court ruled that parents may not use corporal punishment. Among Christians, James Dobson's Dare to Discipline (1970) made the verse a defense of spanking for many evangelicals; William Webb argued that Scripture's own direction moves beyond the rod while keeping its concern for correction. Many churches and child-welfare bodies now urge non-physical discipline (compare Ephesians 6:4). The text itself does not settle the modern debate; it insists that love disciplines.

a: Whoever keeps back his rod hates his son,
t: The rod in the ancient world and in the church
p: Egypt, Ahiqar, the rabbis and the church fathers all took beating for granted in schooling. Some also set limits.
b: Physical punishment was normal in ancient schooling. A text from the Egyptian scribal schools says that a boy's ear is on his back: he listens when he is beaten (the Late Egyptian Miscellanies), and the Aramaic sayings of Ahiqar, found at Elephantine (400s BC), tell a father not to hold back the rod from his son (Story of Ahiqar). The rabbis open the midrash on Exodus with this verse: Abraham's softness spoiled Ishmael, and David's spoiled Absalom and Adonijah (Exodus Rabbah 1:1). Augustine remembered the beatings of his schoolmasters with pain and asked whether they served any good (Confessions, book 1). John Wesley's sermon "On the Education of Children" (1783) urged parents to break a child's self-will early. The text was read in every age; how it was used changed with each.

a: seeks him out early with discipline
p: Shicharo means "seeks him early" or "seeks him eagerly". The KJV's "chasteneth him betimes" means "in good time".
b: The verb shichar is related to shachar, "dawn": to look for someone at first light, and so to seek eagerly (7:15; 8:17: "those who hunt hard for me will find me"). Applied here, the loving parent "seeks him with discipline": he goes after the child's good, and starts early in the child's life (the KJV's "betimes"). Musar is the book's word for discipline (see the note at 1:2), which covers teaching, correction and punishment together, so the second line is wider than the rod. The Greek has "the one who loves him disciplines him with care" (epimelōs).

a: The wisest of women builds her house,
t: The wisest of women, or Wisdom?
p: The Hebrew vowels give chakhmot, "the wisest of women". Pointed chokhmot, the same letters are Wisdom of 9:1.
b: The Leningrad Codex reads chakhmot nashim, "the wise ones of women", the same form as "her wise noblewomen" in Judges 5:29; the Plain follows it: "The wisest of women". Its opposite, 'ivvelet, "folly", may be the foolish woman's own folly or Woman Folly of 9:13–18. The same consonants, pointed chokhmot, are the form used of Lady Wisdom in 1:20 and 9:1 ("Wisdom has built her house"), and many scholars read them that way here, often taking "of women" as a later gloss; then the verse speaks of Wisdom and Folly as in chapter 9 (see the variants). The Greek has "Wise women built houses." Either way, the household's fate is in a woman's hands, a high view of women's work in its world (compare 12:4; 31:10–31).
orig: חַכְמוֹת נָשִׁים בָּנְתָה בֵיתָהּ (chakhmot nashim banetah veitah)

a: puts out a shoot of pride
p: Choter is a shoot or branch (Isaiah 11:1), and also a rod for beating.
b: Choter appears only here and in Isaiah 11:1, "From Jesse's stump a shoot will come out". The fool's mouth sprouts pride like a branch. The word can also mean a stick, and many read "in the mouth of a fool is a rod for his pride" (changing ga'avah, "pride", to gevoh, "his back"): his words bring a beating on himself. The second line has a loose grammar too: the lips of the wise guard "them", either the wise themselves or others.

a: the feed trough stays clean
p: A barn with no oxen is neat, and nothing grows. Bar, "clean", is also the word for grain.
b: Oxen pulled the plow, and plowing made the harvest. A farmer could keep his feed trough clean by not keeping cattle, but he would have no crop. The word bar, "clean", sounds the same as bar, "grain", so the line also hints at an empty manger: no ox, no grain. The saying is a lesson in trade-offs: the mess and cost of the ox are the price of the harvest.

a: Stubborn fools sneer at the guilt offering,
p: The grammar is hard. 'Asham can be guilt or the guilt offering that makes amends.
b: The verb "mocks" is singular and "stubborn fools" is plural, so the line may mean "guilt mocks fools" or "fools, it (guilt) mocks them". 'Asham is guilt and the sacrifice that repairs it, the guilt offering of Leviticus 5:14–6:7, which included paying back what was taken plus a fifth. The Plain reads the plainest sense: fools scoff at making amends, while among the upright there is "goodwill" (ratson), the favor of God and neighbors. The Greek reads "The houses of the lawless will owe purification".

a: Only the heart knows how bitter it feels,
p: No one else can fully share another's sorrow or joy. Solomon's temple prayer says the same.
b: The saying is about the privacy of the inner life. Bitterness and joy are known from inside; an outsider (zar) cannot "mix in" (yit'arav, the word for sharing or taking part). Solomon's prayer at the temple speaks of the person who "knows the wound in his own heart" (1 Kings 8:38), and Paul asks who knows a person's thoughts except the spirit within him (1 Corinthians 2:11). The line is not a call to loneliness; it is a reason for gentleness, since no one sees the whole of another's grief. Christian readers have found comfort in the one who does know the heart (15:11; Hebrews 4:15).

a: There is a road that looks straight to a person,
p: This verse returns word for word at 16:25. A road that seems right can end in death.
b: "Straight" (yashar) is the word for upright. The danger is self-deception: a way can look right "before a person", in his own sight (compare 12:15; 21:2), and still end on "the roads of death". The collectors kept the saying twice (16:25 has the same Hebrew). Judges ends with "Everyone did whatever was right in his own eyes" (Judges 21:25), and Jesus speaks of the broad road that leads to destruction (Matthew 7:13–14). On the two roads in Proverbs, see 4:18–19.

a: A heart that has turned back
p: Sug lev, "one who turns back in heart", is the KJV's "backslider". The second line is unclear.
b: Sug lev is a person whose heart has turned away (compare Psalm 44:18; Psalm 80:18, where the same verb means turning back from God). He will be "stuffed with his own ways", filled with the results of his choices (compare 1:31). The second line, "and a good man from upon him", is hard. Many scholars change one letter to read "from his deeds" (mimma'alalav): the good man is filled with the fruit of his deeds. The Plain keeps the Hebrew and renders "what is his".

a: A naive person trusts every word he hears,
p: The verb is he'emin, "to believe, trust", the word of Genesis 15:6. Faith and gullibility are not the same.
b: The peti, "the naive" (see the note at 1:4), is the young person open to any influence. He "believes" (ya'amin) every word: the same verb as "Abram put his trust in the LORD" (Genesis 15:6). Proverbs does not praise believing as such; it depends on what is believed. The shrewd person "understands his step", checking where he is going. The New Testament's "do not believe every spirit, but test the spirits" (1 John 4:1) is the same caution. The Greek turns peti into "the innocent" (akakos).

a: a fool flares up and feels safe
p: Mit'abber means "to become furious" or "to cross the line", and boteach "to feel secure".
b: The wise man "fears" (here, is wary) and turns from evil; this echoes Job, who "feared God and turned away from evil" (Job 1:1; compare Proverbs 3:7). The fool mit'abber, a verb from the root for "crossing over" that is used for bursting into anger (26:17; Psalm 78:21). Some translate "is reckless", crossing boundaries. Then he is boteach, "confident, feeling safe": he does not see the danger he is in.

a: happy is the one who is kind to the lowly
t: Happy is the one who is kind
p: Despising a neighbor is sin; kindness to the lowly brings happiness. Psalm 41 and the Beatitudes share the shape.
b: The verse sets two attitudes side by side. Looking down on a neighbor is called sin outright (chote'), and the one who "shows favor" (mechonen) to the lowly is called "happy" (ashrei; see the note at 3:13). The verse answers 14:20: people may avoid the poor, but God blesses those who do not. Psalm 41:1 has the same form: "Happy is the one who pays attention to the weak", and the Beatitudes of Matthew 5:3–10 open each line with the Greek of ashrei. On "lowly" and "poor" in the Hebrew margin, see the variant.

a: loyal love and faithfulness
p: Chesed ve'emet is the pair of words that describes God in Exodus 34:6. The Greek doubles the verse and adds "alms".
b: Chesed ve'emet, loyal love and faithfulness, is the pair in God's description of himself: "great in loyal love and faithfulness" (Exodus 34:6). Proverbs asks people to have the same two qualities (3:3; 16:6; 20:28). Here they are what those who "plow up good" (see the note at 12:20) will meet, or what they show. The Greek turns the verse into four lines, and in the last it uses eleēmosynai, "alms", gifts to the poor, beside faithfulness, a sign of how the Greek translators heard chesed.

a: and his children will have a shelter.
p: "His" may be the one who fears the LORD, or the LORD himself, whose children Israel are.
b: The first line has no person in it, only "the fear of the LORD", so "his children" may mean the children of the person who fears the LORD: a parent's reverence becomes a refuge for the family (compare 20:7). Or the nearest "his" is the LORD, and his children are his people (Deuteronomy 14:1: "You are children of the LORD your God", in fresh wording). Both readings fit. Machseh, "shelter", is a Psalms word for God as refuge (Psalm 46:1; Psalm 91:2).

a: The more people there are, the more splendid the king;
t: "In a great people is a king's glory"
p: The rabbis used this line as a rule: a good deed done by many together honors God more.
b: The saying first speaks of politics: a king's glory lies in a large, thriving population, and a ruler with no people is nothing (compare the census of 2 Samuel 24 and Solomon's people, "like the sand beside the sea in number", in 1 Kings 4:20). The rabbis heard "King" as God and made the phrase berov 'am hadrat melekh a principle: it is better for many to do a commandment together, as when one person says a blessing for a whole group (Bavli Berakhot 53a). It is still cited for praying with a congregation rather than alone.

a: Slow to anger means great understanding;
p: "Slow to anger" is a phrase from God's own self-description. Egypt's sages also praised the cool-tempered man.
b: Erekh appayim, literally "long of nostrils", is the phrase of Exodus 34:6, where the LORD calls himself "slow to anger". Proverbs asks the same of people (15:18; 16:32; 19:11; 25:15). The "short of spirit" person, quick to blow up, "lifts folly high": he puts it on show. Egyptian teachers set the "hot man" against the "silent man" in the same way (Amenemope, chapters 2–4 and 9). James 1:19–20 gives the Christian form: "slow to speak, slow to anger".

a: A calm heart is life for the body,
p: Lev marpe' is "a heart of healing": calm, at peace. Qin'ah is jealousy or burning passion.
b: Marpe' is the word for healing in 12:18, 13:17 and 15:4, and it may also mean calm (from rafah, "to relax"). A calm, healthy heart gives "life to the flesh", the whole body. Qin'ah is strong passion: jealousy, envy, zeal. It works like the "rot in the bones" of 12:4, a disease from inside. The sages saw a link between the inner life and bodily health (17:22; 15:13, 30).

a: taunting the one who made them
p: To oppress the poor is to insult God, who made them. The idea runs from Job to Jesus.
b: The saying gives the reason for kindness to the poor: God made them. To crush them is to "taunt" (cheref, to insult, mock) their Maker. 17:5 and 22:2 say the same, and Job asks of his slave, "Did not one Maker shape us both in the womb?" (Job 31:15). The second line turns it around: kindness to the needy honors God. Jesus' parable of the sheep and goats makes the same link: "every time you did it for one of these brothers of mine, even the least of them, you did it for me" (Matthew 25:40). Jewish and Christian teaching on the dignity of the poor both rest on texts like this (compare Genesis 1:27).

a: in his death
p: The Hebrew says the righteous takes refuge in his death. The Greek read "in his integrity".
b: The Masoretic Text reads bemoto, "in his death": even when he dies, the righteous person has a refuge. Read with 12:28 and 15:24, many Jewish and Christian interpreters have heard here a hope that God shelters the righteous beyond death. The Greek has "in his own holiness", which matches a Hebrew betummo, "in his integrity", with two letters reversed; many scholars think that was the original, since Proverbs elsewhere says little about life after death. The Plain follows the Hebrew (see the variant and the note at 12:28).

a: but sin brings peoples shame
p: The word here, chesed, normally means "loyal love". A rare second chesed means "disgrace", and that is the sense here.
b: The Hebrew is vechesed le'ummim chatta't. The usual chesed is "loyal love", but there is a second, rare word chesed, "disgrace", used in Leviticus 20:17: "it is a disgrace". Most translators, ancient and modern, take that sense: sin is a disgrace to any people. The rabbis played on the usual sense: in Bavli Bava Batra 10b the disciples of Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai explain "the kindness of the nations is sin", because their charity is done for self-glory. The first line, "Righteousness lifts a nation high" (in the KJV, "exalteth"), has often been quoted in speeches about national life.

a: The king's favor goes to a servant with good sense,
p: The 'eved of a king is his official. Joseph and Daniel are the Bible's models of the wise servant at court.
b: The king's "servants" were his ministers and officers (see the note at 11:29). Sayings like this one, and the group in 16:10–15, suit a royal court, where many scholars think young officials were trained (see the chapter page). The servant "with good sense" (maskil) wins favor; the one who "brings disgrace" (mevish) feels the king's fury. The same pair of words described a son in 10:5. Joseph (Genesis 41:37–40) and Daniel (Daniel 1:19–20; Daniel 6:3) are the stories of such servants.

a: A soft-spoken answer turns fury back,
p: The Bible's stories show the saying at work: soft words cool anger, and a hard answer splits a kingdom.
b: "Soft" (rakh) means tender, gentle. When the men of Ephraim quarreled with Gideon, his modest answer worked: "Once he said this, their temper toward him cooled down" (Judges 8:3). Abigail's humble words turned David from bloodshed (1 Samuel 25:23–35). Rehoboam did the opposite: "The king gave the people a hard answer" (1 Kings 12:13), and the northern tribes broke away. A "hurtful word" (devar 'etsev, a word that causes pain) makes anger "climb", like a fire flaring up. The Greek adds a first line: "Anger destroys even the sensible."

a: In every place the LORD has his eyes open,
p: God watches both good and evil people. The verb is the one used of a watchman on a wall.
b: Tsofot, "watching", is the verb of the tsofeh, the sentry on a city wall. The picture is not of a spy but of a guard who sees everything, for protection as well as judgment: "For the LORD's eyes roam all over the earth, so that he may show himself strong for those whose hearts are whole toward him" (2 Chronicles 16:9). Psalm 139 and Hebrews 4:13 say that nothing is hidden from him, and the Mishnah teaches, "Know what is above you: an eye that sees, an ear that hears" (Mishnah Avot 2:1). The verse prepares for 15:11.

a: A tongue that heals is a tree of life,
p: Marpe' may mean "healing" or "calm, gentle". Selef is twisting, as in 11:3.
b: Marpe' lashon, "healing of tongue", is a tongue that heals others, or a calm, gentle tongue (see the note at 14:30). It is "a tree of life" (see the note at 11:30). Selef, "crookedness", is the word for the twisting that ruins the treacherous in 11:3; a twisted tongue causes "a break in the spirit", a crushed heart. The Greek has "The healing of the tongue is a tree of life, and the one who keeps it will be filled with spirit."

a: the heart of fools is not firm
p: Lo-khen may mean "not so" (fools do not spread knowledge) or "not firm, not right".
b: The second line ends lo-khen. Read as "not so", it means the heart of fools does not spread knowledge (the KJV's "doeth not so"). Read with ken as an adjective, "right, firm" (as in 11:19), it says the heart of fools is unsteady or not upright. The Plain takes the second reading, which gives "heart" its own statement. The verb in the first line, yezaru, is used for scattering seed or winnowing grain.

a: When the wicked sacrifice, the LORD finds it abhorrent;
p: Proverbs agrees with the prophets: worship without a good life is hateful to God. The Qumran sect quoted this verse.
b: This is the first time Proverbs mentions sacrifice (zevach) in these chapters, and it sides with the prophets. Samuel tells Saul, "Look: listening is better than sacrifice" (1 Samuel 15:22), and Isaiah, Hosea and Amos say God refuses the offerings of people who do injustice (Isaiah 1:11–17; Hosea 6:6; Amos 5:21–24). The prayer of the upright, by contrast, "pleases him". 21:3, 27 and 28:9 add to the theme. The Damascus Document, a rule book of the sect behind the Qumran scrolls, quotes the verse to say that the prayer of the righteous is like an acceptable offering (Damascus Document 11:20–21). Christian traditions have also used it in a debate about works done without faith (see the chapter page).
orig: זֶבַח רְשָׁעִים תּוֹעֲבַת יְהוָה (zevach resha'im to'evat YHWH)

a: Sheol and Abaddon
p: Sheol is the world of the dead; Abaddon, "the place of ruin", is another name for it. Both lie open before God.
b: She'ol is the underworld, the place of the dead (see the gloss). Abaddon, from 'avad, "to perish", is "the place of destruction", a poetic name for the same realm: "Sheol lies naked before him; / there is no cover over Abaddon" (Job 26:6; compare Job 28:22; Psalm 88:11). In Revelation the name becomes a person, the angel of the abyss, "Abaddon" (Revelation 9:11). The verse argues from the greater to the lesser: if the depths of the dead are open to God, how much more the human heart! The same "how much more" form (af ki) is in 11:31; the rabbis called it qal vachomer, "light and heavy".

a: A little, along with the fear of the LORD, is better
p: Egypt's Instruction of Amenemope has two "better" sayings very close to 15:16–17.
b: This is the first of many "better... than" sayings in the collection (compare 12:9; 16:8, 19; 17:1; 19:1). The Instruction of Amenemope, an Egyptian teaching from about 1200–1100 BC, has a pair that matches 15:16–17 in thought and order: "Better is poverty in the hand of the god than riches in the storehouse; better is bread with a happy heart than riches with vexation" (chapter 6, translated in Lichtheim, vol. 2; the second line returns in chapter 13). Israel's sage puts "the fear of the LORD" where Amenemope has "the hand of the god". Because 22:17–24:22 shows clear knowledge of Amenemope, many scholars think these sayings drew on the same tradition; others think the likeness is the common wisdom of the region. See the notes at 22:17.

a: a stall-fed ox
p: Most Israelites ate meat rarely. A fattened ox was food for kings and great celebrations.
b: Daily food was bread, oil, vegetables and fruit. An ox kept in a stall and fattened was a luxury for feasts: Solomon's table had "ten fat oxen" a day (1 Kings 4:23), the medium at Endor killed her fattened calf for Saul (1 Samuel 28:24), and the father in Jesus' parable kills the fattened calf for his son's return (Luke 15:23). "A plate of vegetables" (aruchat yaraq) is a poor man's meal, but with love it is the better feast. 17:1 says the same with a dry crust.

a: a path that is a raised highway
p: Selulah is a road built up and leveled, like the highway of Isaiah 40.
b: Selulah comes from salal, "to heap up": a road built up with earth and stones and cleared, the kind of highway that Isaiah pictures for the return of the exiles (Isaiah 40:3; Isaiah 62:10). The lazy person's road, by contrast, is "like a hedge of thorns": every step is blocked, because he never clears it. The contrast is not lazy and hard-working but lazy and upright: in Proverbs laziness is a moral failing.

a: A wise son makes a father glad,
t: The frame of the first half
p: This line is the same as 10:1. With it, the first half of the collection ends where it began.
b: 15:20a repeats 10:1a word for word, and many scholars see it as a frame: chapters 10–15 open and nearly close with the wise son and his parents. Others think 15:33 or 16:1 is the real seam, because 15:33–16:9 is a cluster of sayings about the LORD. The second line is sharper than 10:1: the foolish man not only grieves his mother, he "looks down on" her, against the command to honor both parents (Exodus 20:12; compare Proverbs 30:17).

a: a word at the right moment, how good it is!
t: The right word at the right time
p: Timing is part of wisdom. Proverbs, Ecclesiastes and Isaiah all praise the well-timed word.
b: "In its time" (be'itto) is the language of Ecclesiastes' "a time to keep quiet and a time to speak" (Ecclesiastes 3:7). 25:11 gives a picture of such a word, and the servant in Isaiah has "a learner's tongue, / so that I can know how to hold up / a tired person with a word" (Isaiah 50:4). The first line may mean the joy of having the right answer, or the joy a good answer gives to others.

a: The road of life runs upward for one with good sense,
p: "Upward" and "Sheol below" may mean simply life and early death, or hint at a life above.
b: Read in its setting, the verse says the wise person's road leads up, away from Sheol, the world of the dead below: wise living keeps a person from an early grave (compare 7:27). Some Jewish and Christian readers have heard more: a road that leads up to God, past death (compare Psalm 16:11: "You let me know the path of life"; Psalm 49:15; Psalm 73:24). Most scholars think the sages meant the first sense, while granting that the picture opened the way for the second (see the note at 12:28). The Greek reads "the thoughts of the sensible are ways of life, so that he may turn aside from Hades and be saved".

a: he makes the widow's boundary stone stand
p: Moving a boundary stone stole land. The Law, the prophets and Egypt's Amenemope forbid it; Amenemope names the widow.
b: Fields were marked by stones (gevul, the boundary or its marker). Shifting one quietly was theft of land, the family's living: "Do not move your neighbor's boundary marker" (Deuteronomy 19:14), and "A curse on anyone who shifts his neighbor's boundary marker!" (Deuteronomy 27:17). A widow had no husband to defend her land in court, so she was easy prey (Isaiah 1:23; Isaiah 10:2). The LORD himself sets her boundary firm. The Instruction of Amenemope has the same pairing: "Do not move the markers on the borders of fields... nor encroach on the boundaries of a widow" (chapter 6). Proverbs repeats the warning in 22:28 and 23:10–11, inside the section that follows Amenemope.

a: one who hates bribes will live
p: Mattanot means "gifts". In court, a gift to a judge was a bribe, and the Law bans it.
b: The greedy man "cuts off a cut" (botsea' batsa'), grabbing unjust gain, and so "stirs up trouble" for his own house (the verb of 11:17, 29). The one who hates "gifts" will live. The Law forbids bribes because "a bribe blinds those who see clearly" (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19), and Samuel's sons fell because "they took bribes and bent justice" (1 Samuel 8:3). Proverbs knows that gifts open doors (17:8; 18:16; 21:14) but condemns the bribe that twists justice (17:23). After this verse the Greek adds the saying the Hebrew has at 16:6: "By alms and faithfulness sins are purged away."

a: the prayers of the righteous he hears
p: God is "far" from the wicked and near to the righteous who pray.
b: "Far" (rachoq) is not distance in space, since 15:3 has just said the LORD's eyes are everywhere. It is distance in relationship: he does not answer the wicked (1:28; 28:9). The Psalms say "The LORD's eyes turn toward the righteous, / and his ears toward their cry for help" (Psalm 34:15), and 1 Peter 3:12 quotes that psalm. James: "the prayer of a righteous person has great power" (James 5:16). After this verse the Greek adds the saying the Hebrew has at 16:8.

a: Shining eyes gladden the heart;
p: Me'or 'enayim may be a bright, friendly face, or simply the sight of light.
b: Me'or 'enayim, "the light of eyes", may be the shining look on someone's face (compare 16:15, "the light of the king's face"), which gladdens the one who sees it; or it may be the joy of seeing at all. Parallel is "good news" (shemu'ah tovah), which "fattens the bones": puts strength and health into a person (see the gloss at 11:25). In the Greek this verse and the rest of chapter 15 are arranged differently (see the note at 15:31).

a: An ear that hears the rebuke that brings life
t: A verse missing from the Greek
p: The Greek of Codex Vaticanus has no 15:31, and it reorders the end of chapter 15 and the start of 16.
b: In the Greek, the last verses of chapter 15 and the first of chapter 16 are arranged differently. Codex Vaticanus, as Swete prints it, places the sayings the Hebrew has at 16:6–9 among and just after 15:27–29, then gives 15:30, 15:32 and 15:33, and has nothing for 15:31. So this verse has no Greek. The Hebrew manuscripts have it. The ear that hears life-giving rebuke "will lodge" (talin, spend the night) among the wise: it belongs in their company.
orig: אֹזֶן שֹׁמַעַת תּוֹכַחַת חַיִּים (ozen shoma'at tokhachat chayyim)

a: The fear of the LORD is wisdom's discipline,
p: The verse ties together the book's motto (1:7) and a saying repeated at 18:12.
b: "The fear of the LORD" (see the note at 1:7) is called musar chokhmah, "the discipline of wisdom": the training that wisdom gives, or the training that leads to it. The second line, "before honor goes humility", returns at 18:12, and 22:4 joins humility and the fear of the LORD again. The verse leads into a run of sayings about the LORD in 16:1–9. Jesus' saying that "the one who brings himself low will be raised up" (Luke 14:11) and Philippians 2:8–9 rest on the same pattern.
orig: יִרְאַת יְהוָה מוּסַר חָכְמָה (yir'at YHWH musar chokhmah)
